questions.prompt: The gradient of \(f\) is Lipschitz continuous with constant \(L\) when, for every pair of points,
questions.explanation: Lipschitz continuity of the gradient bounds how fast the gradient can change. The inequality runs from the gradient difference to \(L\) times the distance. The reversed inequality would be a lower bound on the change. Equal function values are a different condition. A zero Hessian gives \(L = 0\), which is the special case of an affine function, not the definition.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(x_1, x_2) = 3 x_1^2 + x_2^2\). The Hessian is \(\mathrm{diag}(6, 2)\). What Lipschitz constant of the gradient is given by the induced 2-norm of this Hessian?
questions.explanation: For a symmetric matrix the induced 2-norm is the largest absolute eigenvalue. Here the eigenvalues are \(6\) and \(2\), so the norm is \(6\). A constant Hessian equal to that matrix makes \(6\) a sharp Lipschitz constant of the gradient. Reporting \(2\) uses the smaller eigenvalue. Reporting \(8\) adds them. Reporting \(12\) doubles the larger one.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a diagonal array</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">a   0</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   b</text></svg>

questions.prompt: If the induced 2-norm of the Hessian is at most \(L\) at every point of a convex domain, then
questions.explanation: The fundamental theorem along the segment writes the gradient difference as an integral of Hessian-vector products. Bounding each product by the induced norm produces \(\lVert\nabla f(y) - \nabla f(x)\rVert \le L \lVert y - x\rVert\). A constant smaller than the norm is not enough. The gradient is constant only for \(L = 0\). A bound on the Hessian does not make the objective linear.

options: \(L\) is a Lipschitz constant of the gradient
\(L\) is a Lipschitz constant only when it is smaller than every eigenvalue

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that produces a Lipschitz constant from a twice differentiable objective. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The Hessian is the derivative of the gradient, so it comes first. The induced norm turns the matrix into a scalar bound at each point. A single \(L\) has to dominate all of those scalars before it can be called a Lipschitz constant on the whole domain. Choosing \(L\) before the norms are known has nothing to dominate.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a diagonal array</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">a   0</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   b</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A two-by-two array with labels on the diagonal.
steps: At each point, compute the induced 2-norm of that Hessian.
Choose \(L\) at least as large as every one of those norms.
Use that \(L\) as a Lipschitz constant of the gradient.

questions.prompt: The induced 2-norm of the Hessian equals \(5\) at every point. Which numbers are valid Lipschitz constants of the gradient?
questions.explanation:
Any number at least \(5\) works, and a smaller number does not dominate the Hessian norm.
• \(5\), \(5.5\), and \(7\) are large enough.
• \(4\) and \(1\) are strictly below \(5\), so neither is a Lipschitz constant for this gradient.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(x) = \tfrac12 \lVert A x - b\rVert^2\) with the single column \(A = (p, q)\). The Hessian is the scalar \(p^2 + q^2\). A sharp Lipschitz constant of the gradient equals
questions.explanation: The Hessian of \(\tfrac12 \lVert A x - b\rVert^2\) is \(A^T A\). For one column that product is \(p^2 + q^2\), and a \(1 \times 1\) positive semidefinite Hessian has induced norm equal to itself. Both names appear. The sum \(p + q\) forgets the squares. The product \(p q\) is an off-diagonal entry that this one-column Gram matrix does not have. Doubling the sum would be the Hessian of \(\lVert A x - b\rVert^2\) without the one-half.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a diagonal array</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">a   0</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   b</text></svg>

questions.prompt: A note reads a constant Hessian with eigenvalues \(2\) and \(8\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: A symmetric matrix has induced 2-norm equal to its spectral radius, here \(8\). That norm is a sharp Lipschitz constant, and every larger number is also valid. The false step uses the smaller eigenvalue. The value \(2\) does not dominate a Hessian that stretches by \(8\).
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a long ellipse</title><line x1="28" y1="104" x2="256" y2="104"/><polygon points="256,104 249.6,106.7 249.6,101.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="140" y1="186" x2="140" y2="24"/><polygon points="140,24 142.7,30.4 137.3,30.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="250" y="120" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="148" y="20" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><ellipse cx="140" cy="104" rx="86" ry="46"/><line x1="54" y1="104" x2="226" y2="104" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="140" y1="58" x2="140" y2="150" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: An axis-aligned ellipse, longer along the first axis.
steps: The Hessian is symmetric, with eigenvalues \(2\) and \(8\).
Its induced 2-norm is the largest absolute eigenvalue, which is \(8\).
The Lipschitz constant of the gradient is the smallest eigenvalue, \(2\).
Any number at least \(8\), for instance \(10\), is also a Lipschitz constant of this gradient.
reasons: The smallest eigenvalue does not dominate the Hessian. The induced norm is \(8\).
The induced 2-norm is the smallest eigenvalue.
A number larger than \(8\) cannot be a Lipschitz constant.

questions.prompt: Let \(f(x) = \tfrac12 \lVert A x - b\rVert^2\) with \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). The Gram matrix \(A^T A\) equals \(\mathrm{diag}(5, 1)\). What is a sharp Lipschitz constant of the gradient?
questions.explanation: The Hessian is \(A^T A\), with eigenvalues \(5\) and \(1\). The induced 2-norm is \(5\), and that is the sharp Lipschitz constant. The same number is the square of the largest singular value of \(A\): the column norms lead to singular values \(\sqrt{5}\) and \(1\), and \((\sqrt{5})^2 = 5\). Reporting \(1\) uses the smaller eigenvalue. Reporting \(6\) adds the diagonal entries. Reporting \(\sqrt{5}\) stops at the singular value and forgets the square.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a diagonal array</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">a   0</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   b</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A two-by-two array with labels on the diagonal.

questions.prompt: For \(f(x) = \tfrac12 \lVert A x - b\rVert^2\), a sharp Lipschitz constant of the gradient is
questions.explanation: The Hessian is \(A^T A\), whose eigenvalues are the squares of the singular values of \(A\). The induced 2-norm of the Hessian is therefore \(\sigma_{\max}(A)^2 = \lVert A\rVert_2^2\). The singular value without the square is the norm of \(A\), not of \(A^T A\). The smallest singular value bounds nothing from above. The vector \(b\) shifts the residual and does not appear in the Hessian.

questions.prompt: A quadratic upper bound that uses this Lipschitz constant is
questions.explanation: Once the gradient is Lipschitz with constant \(L\), integrating the remainder produces a quadratic upper model with coefficient \(L/2\). That upper bound is the descent lemma. First-order convexity is a linear lower bound and does not use \(L\). The upper model does not force \(f\) to be constant. The normal equations are a stationarity condition for least squares.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 300 230" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>nested contours</title><line x1="28" y1="118" x2="272" y2="118"/><polygon points="272,118 265.6,120.7 265.6,115.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="150" y1="204" x2="150" y2="26"/><polygon points="150,26 152.7,32.4 147.3,32.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="266" y="134" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="158" y="30" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><ellipse cx="150" cy="118" rx="40" ry="24"/><ellipse cx="150" cy="118" rx="72" ry="44"/><ellipse cx="150" cy="118" rx="104" ry="62"/></svg>

options: the normal equations of a linear program
the descent lemma, \(f(y) \le f(x) + \nabla f(x)^T(y - x) + (L/2)\lVert y - x\rVert^2\)
the first-order convexity inequality, which runs the other way

questions.prompt: Let \(f(t) = 2 t^2\), so \(f'(t) = 4t\). What is \(\lvert f'(3) - f'(1)\rvert \,/\, \lvert 3 - 1\rvert\)?
questions.explanation: The derivatives are \(f'(3) = 12\) and \(f'(1) = 4\). The absolute difference is \(8\), and the distance is \(2\), so the quotient is \(4\). The second derivative is the constant \(4\), which is why every such quotient equals \(4\). Reporting \(8\) stops before dividing by the distance. Reporting \(2\) is the distance. Reporting \(12\) is one derivative.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping upward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: A local quadratic rate for Newton's method asks this Lipschitz idea of
questions.explanation: The standard local analysis assumes the Hessian itself is Lipschitz near a point where it is positive definite. That bounds how fast the Newton correction changes, and it is what produces the quadratic rate. The objective value is not the object of that hypothesis. An Armijo parameter is at most 1. The simplex ratio test belongs to linear programming.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
options: the Hessian, so the derivative of the Newton map stays controlled near a minimizer
the objective value alone, with no derivative
